title: Replication
summary: Keep copies of the database on several machines — for more reads and for survival.

goals.text: Leaders, followers and the replication log
Analytics replicas, backups and replication styles

steps.title: One database, doing everything
body: Every read and every write goes to a single database server. It’s 90% busy — and most of that is reads: product pages, profiles, feeds.
It’s also a single point of failure: if it dies, so does everything.

callout.text: Most apps read far more than they write — often 10 or 100 reads per write.

steps.title: Keep copies: leader and followers
body: Add two followers (replicas). The leader still takes every write, and streams each change to the followers through a replication log.
Each follower replays the changes and ends up with the same data.

callout.text: Also called primary/replica or master/slave. Built into PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB and most others.

steps.title: Send reads to the followers
body: Now the app sends reads to the followers and only writes to the leader. Read capacity doubles — two machines now do nothing but reads — and the leader cools down to 30%.
Need more reads? Add another follower.

callout.text: This works brilliantly for read-heavy apps. It doesn’t help write-heavy ones — every write still goes through one leader.

steps.title: Copies lag behind
body: Replication is usually asynchronous: the leader confirms a write right away and ships it to followers a moment later.
Alice renames herself, then reloads her profile. The read lands on a follower that hasn’t caught up — she sees her old name and thinks the save failed.

callout.text: Lag is normally milliseconds, but under load it can grow to seconds or minutes.

changes: − Follower still has the old one

steps.title: Read your own writes
body: A common fix: for a few seconds after someone writes, send their reads to the leader. Everyone else keeps using followers.
The other option is synchronous replication: the leader waits for a follower to confirm before saying “saved”. No lag — but slower writes, and they stall if that follower is down.

callout.text: For data you can’t afford to lose, a common setup is one synchronous follower (for safety) and the rest asynchronous (for speed). Many systems stay fully asynchronous and accept losing the last moments of writes in a crash.

steps.title: The leader dies
body: The leader crashes. Reads keep working — the followers still have the data — but every write now fails. Nobody can sign up, post or pay.

callout.text: Followers protect your reads. Writes need a new leader.

steps.title: Failover: promote a follower
body: Failover: the most up-to-date follower is promoted to leader, the app points its writes there, and the other follower replicates from it. A fresh follower is added to restore the spare.
Writes resume within seconds to a minute. Any writes the old leader hadn’t shipped yet may be lost — another reason to keep one follower synchronous.

The hard part is being sure the leader is dead. If it was only slow or cut off, you now have two leaders both accepting writes — split brain. Doing this safely takes a majority vote: see Consensus & Leader Election.

callout.text: Same idea as the standby load balancer: a spare that takes over. Managed databases automate it.

steps.title: Case: the 20-minute report
body: The finance team runs a monthly report — a 20-minute query that scans years of orders. They point it at a follower, and that follower, which also serves the app’s reads, grinds to a halt and falls minutes behind.
Fix: a dedicated analytics replica that the app never reads from. Heavy queries can be as slow as they like there.

callout.text: At larger scale, copy data into a separate analytics warehouse (BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift) built for huge scans.

changes: + Analytics replica, outside the app’s read pool
~ Reports no longer slow the app

steps.title: Case: the migration with no WHERE
body: A deploy runs a migration with a missing WHERE: UPDATE users SET email = NULL. The leader obeys — and replication faithfully copies the mistake to every follower within a second.

Replicas protect you from a machine failing, not from a bad write. For that you need backups: a nightly snapshot plus the archived write log, which together can rebuild the database as it was at any chosen moment — point-in-time recovery.

callout.text: A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a backup. Rehearse restores, and know how long one takes.

changes: ~ Restore to 14:02, a minute before the mistake

steps.title: Three ways to replicate
body: Everything so far was single-leader: one writer, many readers. It’s simple and it’s what most SQL databases do.

Multi-leader puts a leader in each region so writes stay local — at the cost of conflicts when two regions edit the same row. Leaderless systems (Cassandra, Riak, ScyllaDB — the “Dynamo-style” databases) write to several copies at once and read from several — the quorums in the CAP lesson.

callout.text: Prefer single-leader until you have a concrete reason (global writes, extreme availability) to take on conflict handling.

lines: leaderless     write N, read R · quorums

steps.title: Recap
body:
• A leader takes writes and streams them to followers.
  • Followers scale reads and survive losing a machine.
  • Async replicas lag: route a user’s reads to the leader right after they write.
  • When the leader dies, fail over to a follower.
  • Keep heavy analytics on its own replica.
  • Replicas are not backups: keep snapshots and rehearse restoring them.

callout.text: Next up: Sharding — for when even the leader can’t keep up with the writes.
